item.title: How Dhruv Sayani built Ccigmaa Lifestyles into a five-brand personal care business
item.description:
How Dhruv Sayani built Ccigmaa Lifestyle into a four-brand personal care business

item.content:encoded:
Hair and water composition can change significantly every 100 kilometres across India, affecting how haircare products perform. It was this observation, made while researching premature greying in his 20s, that led Dhruv Sayani to build Ccigmaa Lifestyles, a Mumbai-based personal care company.

Sayani found that keratin, the protein that makes up most of human hair, responds differently to these regional variations, something he believed conventional haircare formulations did not adequately address.

In 2018, he launched KT Professional, a salon-focused haircare brand developed specifically for stylists. Since then, Ccigmaa Lifestyles has expanded its portfolio with three more brands, KT Men, KT Kids and KT Derma, each focused on specific personal care needs.

The company, founded in 2018, aims to inspire “millions of minds” through Indian-made personal care products, according to Sayani.

Build credibility before distribution

Proving the regional-formulation premise required evidence a lab alone could not generate.

Rather than build retail distribution first and let salons discover the brand afterward, Ccigmaa Lifestyles went the other way around, giving hairstylists across Indian cities access to formulations, and letting their feedback, not a marketing brief, decide what shipped outside the production.

KT Professional was launched with Rs 30 lakh of the founder’s personal savings in 2018, exactly that route. Nearly a decade later, the company works with more than 27,000 salons across 86 cities, a distribution footprint built one stylist and salon relationship at a time rather than through a single national launch mode.

Turn specialization into a growth engine

Once KT Professional’s salon-first model was validated, the more conventional path was to push that single brand harder, deeper into more cities, more product lines, more advertising.

Sayani chose a different growth mechanism instead: apply the same underlying logic, that a mass-market, one-size-fits-all product underserves a large share of its actual buyers, to categories beyond haircare.

That decision produced KT Men and KT Kids as standalone brands rather than product extensions, a materially harder path since each requires its own credibility, its own distribution relationships, and its own reason to exist, rather than borrowing KT Professional's. It is also, by most available market evidence, the better-timed one.

Redseer projects India’s beauty and personal care market reaching $40 billion by 2030, positioning India as the fourth largest such market globally, with Gen Z and Alpha consumers becoming the largest beauty-spending cohort in that growth. A market moving toward younger, more specific buyers rewards brands built around a defined need far more than it rewards a single brand trying to serve everyone.

Position KT Men around performance, not vanity

Sayani says most Indian grooming brands have built their positioning around attraction or plain cosmetic vanity rather than performance, a framing he believed increasingly out of step with younger, fitness-oriented male consumers.

KT Men was built to compete on the second premise instead of the first, launching at an accessible Rs 399 entry point before extending into a higher Rs 699 to Rs 999 band through its G.O.A.T Edition range, a licensing partnership with the Argentina Football Association built around Lionel Messi, Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez.

The brand has since disclosed a Rs 36 Crore marketing investment behind that range, against a Rs 200 crore revenue target over 18 to 24 months, sitting on top of KT Men’s original Rs 100 crore first-year ambition. Whether that specific target lands on schedule matters less to the decision itself than the positioning bet underneath it, that performance, not image, was the underused argument in Indian men's grooming.

Design for two customers at once

Children’s personal care carries a structural complication most categories do not: the person buying the product and the person using it are rarely evaluating it the same way.

A parent checks an ingredient list and asks whether a formulation is genuinely mild enough for a child's skin. A child has no interest in either question and decides on nothing more sophisticated than whether the experience of using it was enjoyable.

Rather than let KT Professional’s existing haircare range absorb a children's line as a smaller variant, Ccigmaa built KT Kids as its own brand, formulated specifically for children rather than adapted from adult products, and has run two entertainment-licensing partnerships in 15 months, first with SpongeBob SquarePants, then with Peppa Pig, timed separately rather than bundled, each aimed at a distinct age band.

The decision to treat that dual-audience problem as its own category, rather than a footnote inside an existing one, is the same underlying instinct that produced KT Men, applied to a harder version of the same question.

The company created five brands with one method to connect them: identify a specific need a generalist product is failing to serve, validate the idea against real, direct feedback before scaling it, and build a dedicated brand around it rather than stretch an existing one to cover it.

Ccigmaa's next test is whether that method holds as a repeatable business engine rather than a run of good individual calls, since a Rs 40 billion market moving toward specificity will reward the companies that can keep making this decision correctly, not just the ones that made it once.

item.title: Six Indian startups selected for Hub71's Immersion Programme in Abu Dhabi
item.description: The winners were chosen from among ten finalists in the areas of AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and digital finance.
item.content:encoded:
Six Indian startups have been selected for Hub71's Immersion Programme in Abu Dhabi, following the UAE-India Start-Up Series 2.0 finale in Bengaluru.

Hub71, Abu Dhabi's global tech ecosystem, is the cross-border partner which will connect the startups with investors, corporate and government partners, regulators, and prospective customers.

Convened by the UAE Embassy in New Delhi, the series drew more than 11,000 applications this year. The winners were chosen from among ten finalists in the areas of artificial intelligence, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and digital finance.

Since the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement came into force in 2022, bilateral trade between India and the UAE has grown from about $73 billion to more than $101 billion, it added. Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of UAE, and Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India, have set a target of $200 billion by 2032.

According to a statement, the series seeks to help Indian companies expand globally, with the UAE as their gateway to investment and growth, said a statement.

H.E. Abdulla Saif Al Nuaimi, Ambassador of the UAE to India, announced the winners. Three of them will be shortlisted for Hub71's Access Programme; one startup will join the programme and receive AED 250,000 in in-kind incentives and AED 250,000 in cash through a SAFE note, the statement said.

Al Nuaimi said, “The UAE and India have set themselves the goal of doubling bilateral trade to $200 billion by 2032. Innovative companies like the ones we celebrate tonight will be central to reaching it. The UAE offers Indian founders a gateway to new markets, capital, and partnerships, and we will support these winners as they grow there. I congratulate all ten finalists on the standard they set.”

Ahmad Ali Alwan, CEO of Hub71, said, “India is an important source of technology innovation and entrepreneurial talent, and our collaboration with the UAE-India Start-Up Series is helping more ambitious founders connect with investors, partners, and market opportunities through Hub71.

"Through Hub71's Immersion Programme, startups can deepen their understanding of the market, build meaningful relationships, and access opportunities that support their growth in the UAE and internationally.”

The finale in Bengaluru brought together 10 startups for two days of investor meetings, mentorship and live pitching: CYRAN AI Solutions, Nawgati, KoinX, Onsite, Forthcode, Flo Mobility, Pointo, Econovus, XYMA Analytics, and Sustvest.

The jury comprised Al Nuaimi; Tushar Ved, President of Apparel Group; and members of the UAE-India business community. Al Nuaimi also unveiled a Top 50 Investment Dossier profiling 50 leading applicants.

The six winners will take part in a two-week hybrid programme, comprising a week of virtual preparation, followed by a one-week in-person session at Hub71 in Abu Dhabi from December 7. The programme includes mentorship, curated introductions, and knowledge sessions on Abu Dhabi's business and regulatory environment.

The first edition in 2025 opened a pathway for Indian startups to explore the UAE through Hub71. Endimension, an AI-powered radiology platform, later joined Hub71's Access Programme as part of Cohort 18. BioReform, Docket Run, Data Sutram and SBNRI are the other startups that have completed the Immersion Programme.

Here's a look at the six winning startups this year.

CYRAN AI Solutions (New Delhi, NCR)

The deeptech company uses AI to help aerospace and precision manufacturers catch defects before a part ships, an engine returns to service, or a satellite launches. Founded by IIT Delhi professor Manan Suri, it also builds edge AI for Industry 4.0 and geospatial customers.

Nawgati (Noida, Uttar Pradesh)

The AI and IoT platform helps fuel companies, dealers and governments monitor and run fuel stations from one real-time view. Founded by Aalaap Nair, Vaibhav Kaushik and Aryan Sisodia, the startup raised $2.5 million in a pre-Series A round led by Ajay Upadhyaya, and has deployments in Sri Lanka and the UAE.

KoinX (Bhubaneswar, Odisha)

This crypto tax and accounting platform helps investors and businesses calculate their tax, track their holdings, and keep compliant books. Founded in 2022 by Punit Agarwal, its CEO, the startup raised $1.5 million in seed funding from investors including Polygon founder Sandeep Nailwal, and later attracted investment from CoinDCX Ventures.

KoinX Founder and CEO Punit Agarwal, told YourStory that he has been active in crypto for about 10 years and had previously led the Crypto Relief Fund, a UAE-domiciled fund of close to $500 million. He said India has the most stringent crypto tax regime in the world, and the crypto market would grow in the country with regulations.

Agarwal said KoinX first earned revenue in the June-July 2023 tax season. Revenue grew from about $140,000 in its first year to about $700,000 in the third. He expects about $1.5 million this financial year, aided by B2B contracts.

In the UAE, KoinX sells B2B software to businesses. Agarwal said a local presence, through Hub71's Immersion Programme, would help build trust.

Onsite (New Delhi, NCR)

The AI-powered construction management platform helps contractors and developers control cost and time from site to office. Founded in March 2021 by Sumit Garg, Dheeraj Anand, and Akshansh Agarwal, the startup raised $1.5 million in 2022 in a round led by Foundamental.

Forthcode (Bengaluru, Karnataka)

The aviation technology company helps airlines grow ancillary revenue and automate operations at the airport, on board, and after the flight. Its platform automates inflight retail, services, and catering management. It has partnered with Worldline for inflight payments in India.

Founder and CEO Ajith Balakumar, told YourStory that Forthcode has built an AI model for aviation on Core42's sovereign AI models. Core42 is an Abu Dhabi-based technology company.

On seatback screens in planes, passengers can search for films or ask advanced questions, such as what a city they are flying over looked like 2,000 years ago. He said the software is isolated from avionics and flight controls, and guardrails limit questions to movies, food and the destination.

Balakumar said AI can also answer queries from ground staff on matters such as dangerous goods compliance and support ancillary revenue and disruption management.

Forthcode is a winner of AviationX Labs by Emirates, Thales, Collins, GE and Airbus, has completed a paid pilot with Emirates, and works with Thales as its go-to-market partner.

Flo Mobility (Bengaluru, Karnataka)

Founded by Manesh Jain and Pratik Patel, the construction robotics company helps builders and contractors move materials across large sites using autonomous electric vehicles.

The startup's Flo Hauler robot can carry up to 1.5 tonnes. More than 60 of its robots are deployed across 10 states for developers including L&T and Godrej Properties. Flo Mobility raised $2.5 million in a pre-Series A round co-led by Mela Ventures and Arali Ventures.

item.title: ‘My dream is to make WeWork India the default choice for workspaces’
item.description: CEO and Managing Director Karan Virmani speaks to YourStory about WeWork India's first year as a public company, its expanding product portfolio, the impact of AI, market opportunities, and his ambitions for the business.
item.content:encoded:
A year after WeWork India announced its IPO in October 2025, CEO and Managing Director Karan Virwani is satisfied with the company’s performance despite a subdued market.

“I think from an investor standpoint and a shareholder standpoint, we've done good. And if you compare it to the relative market, I think we've done really well,” he tells YourStory.

Virwani says founders spend much of their time raising funds and ensuring they have enough liquidity to sustain their businesses. Going public, he believes, removes some of that pressure, allowing them to focus on execution and growth.

“WeWork India has grown by 30%, both from a revenue perspective and an EBITDA perspective. Our digital products also crossed an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 100 crore. So we are doing pretty well,” he says. 

Also Read
How flexible workspaces are changing the way companies think about offices

Launching Rivet and expanding the product portfolio

Virwani says WeWork India’s digitally enabled products, including Virtual Office and Workplace, have performed well. The company earns more than Rs 100 crore in subscription revenue, with the business growing 30% year on year.

“We have been noticing this post COVID. People have been using our spaces on-demand, sort of like how one uses Uber. We own the plug-and-play co-working space sector completely. There’s no major competitor really,” he says.

The company’s managed offices business, which was a new vertical a few years ago, has also expanded.

“It’s grown to become 25% of our business. We did some really large deals this year with big players like T-Mobile, JPMorgan and Amazon.”

WeWork India recently launched Rivet, its design-and-build vertical, to serve existing customers who started with smaller workspaces but now require larger offices.

“Rivet was a way for us to take what they love about WeWork and design-build it for them specifically, based on their requirements and branding,” Virwani says.

He believes Rivet differs from other design-and-build companies because WeWork India also operates physical workspaces, rather than focusing solely on designing and handing over offices.

Working with GCCs and adopting AI

In its early years, particularly 2017 and 2018, WeWork India primarily catered to startups and freelancers. Today, nearly 50% of its business comes from global capability centres (GCCs), including large, mid-sized and smaller operations.

“A lot of these GCCs are in an exploratory phase when they enter a country like India. They’re starting or they’re testing if they can hire. They’re really seeing if this offshoring model works for them,” Virwani says.

He cites the example of Moss Adams, which has since merged with Baker Tilly under the latter’s name.

“They started with us with like 25 seats and now we've done a 600-person managed office for them. All in a span of roughly two years.” 

Virwani is also optimistic about the opportunities created by AI. He says WeWork India has seen an acceleration in demand from a new group of AI-focused companies that have become its customers.

He believes AI is increasing the need for collaboration and, in turn, collaborative workspaces. He also expects entrepreneurship to grow faster over the next three years than it has in the previous three, as technology makes it easier for more people to start businesses.

“Those entrepreneurs will either join mid-sized businesses, smaller businesses, or they'll start their own businesses. And that will definitely benefit us because that's the type of audience that we're aimed at,” he says. 

WeWork India has also introduced AI into its own operations, from routine tasks to more advanced applications. These include spatial analytics using CCTV footage to understand how people use its offices and improve workspace design.

“Contrary to popular belief, AI is not actually reducing our employee headcount. It's not like I can let go of a few hundred people. In fact, it's making everyone much more proactive. The quality of output has definitely increased,” he says.

Also Read
WeWork India strengthens leadership with key board appointments

Expansion plans and bigger ambitions

WeWork India currently operates across eight metropolitan markets: Bengaluru, Mumbai, Gurugram, New Delhi, Noida, Hyderabad, Chennai, and Pune.

Virwani says the company will consider expanding into other cities and towns when there is sufficient demand.

“I don't view it as Tier II or Tier III. Tomorrow, if any city starts to show a type of demand, which is a combination of enterprise and startups, and there is good supply coming in, we would 100% look at it as a serious growth city,” he explains.

For now, however, he would prefer to expand into areas on the outskirts of Bengaluru rather than enter an entirely new city. The priority is to operate where demand and supply are concentrated.

According to Cushman & Wakefield’s Global Trends in Flexible Office 2026 report, India ranks as the world’s most mature flexible office market.

Virwani expects the Indian market to double over the next five years.

“I really see the overall industry doubling in the next five years, which will mean that it’s roughly growing at about 20-odd per cent year on year. I see us trying to beat that growth, and so the business itself will more than double in that time period.”

He says WeWork India is evolving from a coworking space provider into an end-to-end real estate services platform.

While the flexible workspace sector has relatively low entry barriers, Virwani believes scaling a business remains difficult. He also sees enough room in the market for WeWork India and its major competitors to grow.

His mid-term ambition is to increase WeWork India’s market capitalisation from around Rs 10,000 crore to closer to Rs 50,000 crore.

“My aim or my dream would be that WeWork India becomes just the default. When you think of a workspace, you think of us,” Virmani says.

Edited by Teja Lele

item.title: Karnataka emerges as India's GCC powerhouse with 1,088 centres, says Kharge
item.description: Karnataka hosts 51% of India's GCCs and 43% of its GCC AI talent. Minister Priyank Kharge unveiled a new Zinnov-KDEM report at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Global companies are increasingly looking to their India offices to do more than support business operations. In Karnataka, these centres are taking on a larger role in building and deploying artificial intelligence for their global businesses.

The State is home to 1,088 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), accounting for 51% of India's total. It also hosts 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, representing 43% of the country's GCC AI/ML talent.

These findings are part of a new report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, released by Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank M. Kharge on November 19 at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.

Prepared by Zinnov in collaboration with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), the report examines how GCCs in the State are building AI capabilities, hiring specialised talent and taking on larger technology mandates.

Karnataka leads in AI maturity

The report finds that surveyed Karnataka GCCs score 1.12 times the national average in overall AI maturity. Around 66% have reached the Portfolio Hub stage, compared with approximately 43% across India.

The findings also point to stronger AI adoption within these centres. Around 69% of surveyed Karnataka GCCs have dedicated AI budgets, against 57% nationally. Similarly, 69% conduct role-specific AI training, compared with 53% across the country.

Around 83% reuse in-house AI platforms across business units, while 66% follow Responsible AI practices. The corresponding national figures are 57% and 49%, respectively.

Karnataka's position is also reflected in its AI infrastructure. More than 660 GCCs in the State have AI and machine learning capabilities, while over 120 dedicated AI and ML Centres of Excellence operate in the region. This represents around 48% of India's total.

Bengaluru attracts AI leadership talent

Beyond infrastructure and adoption, Bengaluru has emerged as a major destination for senior AI talent.

The city accounts for 44% of India's senior AI leadership job postings within GCCs, 6.4 times the average of other tier-I cities. It also accounts for up to 63% of Distinguished and Principal AI Engineer openings.

In 2026, AI skills featured in 13.6% of GCC job postings in Bengaluru, compared with 9.8% at the same companies' offices outside Karnataka.

The State's wider technology ecosystem supports this demand. Karnataka hosts more than 29% of India's AI startups and has over 5,000 active technology investors. It also produces more than 130,000 STEM graduates annually.

GCCs move beyond support roles

The report outlines five priorities for Karnataka's GCC ecosystem through 2030. These include attracting advanced GCC mandates, increasing global ownership of AI development, building AI leadership talent, scaling AI with measurable business outcomes and moving research into enterprise adoption.

The State currently hosts 1,088 GCCs, including 320 centres belonging to Global 2000 companies. Between FY2021 and FY2026, it attracted 217 of India's 510 new GCCs.

Launching the report, Kharge said Karnataka's GCCs were becoming key drivers of the State's technology leadership.

"With 1,088 GCCs and 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, Karnataka is where global enterprises come to build AI," he said.

He added that the State would continue strengthening AI capabilities, research and skills through its dedicated GCC Policy and IT Policy 2025-30, while extending opportunities to other regions through the Beyond Bengaluru initiative.

Dr Manjula N, Secretary of the Department of Electronics, IT and BT, said Karnataka had embedded AI and deep technology across six State technology policies. She pointed to the higher adoption of role-specific AI training and Responsible AI practices among surveyed GCCs as evidence of this progress.

Nitika Goel, CMO and Managing Partner at Zinnov, said GCCs were entering a new phase in which their value would be measured by AI deployed in production rather than pilots and proofs of concept.

"The contest now is for talent, and Karnataka holds a rare advantage, with over a thousand GCCs, tier-1 academic institutions and the country's largest cohort of start-ups," she said.

The report also points to the State's efforts to build its talent pipeline through Nipuna Karnataka, a Rs 300 crore industry-driven programme focused on AI, deep tech and cybersecurity.

The report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, is available on the KDEM website.

item.title: AI can write code, but knowing what to build still matters
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Srinivas Chamarthy of Diligent India, Madhusudan N. Murthy of EY GDS, and Arun Kalyanaraman of Target discussed why domain expertise, engineering skills, and human judgement remain important as AI makes software development more accessible.
item.content:encoded:
AI is making it easier to build software. Product managers, designers, and domain experts can now turn ideas into prototypes without necessarily knowing how to code. But turning those prototypes into reliable products that solve real problems remains a challenge.

At TechSparks 2026, Srinivas Chamarthy, Senior Vice President of Engineering, Site Lead and Country Head at Diligent India; Madhusudan N. Murthy, Digital Engineering and Tech Strategy Leader at EY GDS; and Arun Kalyanaraman, VP of Engineering at Target in India, discussed these changes during a panel titled ‘From Who Can Code to Who Can Build’.

The discussion was moderated by Chhavi Mahajan, Chief Content Officer at YourStory.

From prototypes to production

AI-assisted development allows business teams to test ideas, demonstrate concepts, and gather feedback much earlier. However, a prototype that shows an idea can work is not necessarily ready for production. Applications still need to meet security, scalability, and reliability requirements.

Murthy said that AI is making experimentation easier, but companies must distinguish between a proof of concept and a production-ready application. Engineering teams still need to identify vulnerabilities, put safeguards in place, and ensure systems can handle real-world use.

“It's good, it's a very positive development, but it also has to have its guardrails,” he stated.

Kalyanaraman said AI can do more than help developers write code faster. It can also speed up the entire development process, from defining a problem and testing a solution to getting stakeholder approval. However, strong engineering fundamentals, architectural thinking, and technical depth will remain essential, even as AI changes how solutions are built.

He gave the example of a product owner, an engineer, and a UX professional who used AI tools and large language models to prototype a complex concept and present it to leadership within a week. Without these tools, the process could have taken six weeks to two months.

The benefit was not just faster coding, but the ability to test an idea and make a decision sooner.

Chamarthy said coding is becoming a commodity in the generative AI era, shortening the path from prototype to customer feedback to production, with a nine-month cycle potentially coming down to a month or two. As speed increases, he said, knowing what not to build becomes more valuable, so ideas should be tested in a sandbox while experienced engineers harden them for security, scalability, and privacy.

Deciding where human oversight is needed

As companies move from using AI to assist developers to deploying agents that can complete tasks with limited supervision, they must decide how much autonomy to allow.

Chamarthy said this should depend on the risks involved, the potential impact of a decision, and whether its outcome can be reversed.

He suggested organizations consider whether a decision is a two-way-door or a one-way-door call, with significant financial or strategic decisions needing human oversight and contextual judgment.

Chamarthy cautioned that access to AI coding tools cannot replace engineering experience. Experienced engineers understand the architectural decisions that affect security, scalability, and long-term maintenance, including risks that may not be apparent in a prototype.

His advice was to encourage experimentation, but within controlled environments.

“Don't stop the code. Sandbox it.”

This allows more employees to test ideas while giving engineering teams the opportunity to review the applications, address weaknesses, and prepare them for production.

Why domain expertise matters

As AI makes it easier to generate code and find answers, knowing which problems to solve becomes more important.

Kalyanaraman compared using AI to consulting a genie that grants only three wishes. Getting a useful result depends on asking the right questions and understanding the constraints.

“In a world where maybe getting answers are easy, asking the right questions is going to be a really, really critical skill,” he said.

People who understand customers, business processes, and operational requirements are better placed to identify solutions that create value.

Engineering teams will also need systems thinking and platform expertise to help non-engineers develop applications without putting production systems at risk.

The shift also has implications for workforce development.

Murthy said EY GDS is preparing employees for an AI-driven workplace by bringing experienced professionals and younger talent together. Existing employees bring knowledge of customers and systems, while newer team members contribute fresh approaches and develop emerging technical skills.

Chamarthy said teams need a mix of strengths: organizations should upskill existing employees, who understand their products and customers, while bringing in fresh graduates who can work with AI tools.

He also added that engineering performance should be measured by the problems teams solve for customers, rather than only by metrics such as lines of code written or tickets closed.

As AI takes over more routine work, the outcomes delivered by engineering teams become a more useful measure of their contribution.

A workforce of people and AI agents

The panellists expect employees and AI agents to work increasingly closely together.

As agents take on more complex tasks, companies will need to rethink workflows, accountability and performance expectations. They will also need to ensure safeguards keep pace with what the technology can do.

Murthy described a future in which managers will oversee AI agents alongside human employees.

“The future I see is getting used to agents reporting to you and not just humans,” he said.

Kalyanaraman added that The New Tech Order is not just about what AI can do for us. It is about how we evolve our thinking, engineering practices, and decision-making to make the most of it.

While AI is making software easier to build, companies will still need engineering expertise, domain knowledge, and human judgement to decide which ideas are worth pursuing and which prototypes are ready for production.

item.title: 7 Micro-habits under 5 minutes that can change your year
item.description: Discover 7 simple micro-habits that take less than five minutes but can improve your productivity, mindset, health and daily routine.
item.content:encoded:
Big changes do not always require big efforts. Sometimes, the smallest actions repeated every day can make the biggest difference in how you think, work and live. You do not necessarily need an elaborate morning routine, hours of exercise or a complete lifestyle transformation to become a better version of yourself.

A few intentional minutes each day can be enough to build habits that gradually improve your life.

The problem is that many people wait for the perfect time to make a change. They plan to start exercising next Monday, begin reading when work becomes less hectic or organise their lives at the beginning of a new month. However, waiting for the right moment often delays progress.

This is where micro-habits become useful. These are small, simple actions that require very little time and effort but can create meaningful changes when practised consistently. Most can be completed in under five minutes, making them easier to fit into even the busiest schedules.

7 Micro-habits under 5 minutes to improve your daily routine

1. Make your bed every morning

Making your bed may seem like an insignificant task, but it gives you an opportunity to begin your day by completing something simple. Instead of leaving your room untidy, spend two minutes arranging your pillows, straightening your bedsheet and organising your sleeping space.

This small action creates a sense of order and can encourage you to approach other tasks with the same mindset. It is not about having a perfectly organised room but about developing the habit of starting your day with a small accomplishment.

2. Write down three priorities for the day

Before getting distracted by messages, notifications and other responsibilities, take two minutes to identify the three most important things you want to accomplish. These could include completing a work assignment, studying a particular topic or making time for exercise.

Writing down your priorities helps you approach the day with greater clarity instead of reacting to everything that demands your attention. It also makes it easier to recognise what deserves your time and energy.

3. Read two pages of a book

Reading regularly does not require spending an hour with a book every day. Start by reading just two pages whenever you find a few free minutes. You can do this after breakfast, during a break or before going to bed.

Over time, these small reading sessions can help you develop a consistent reading habit and gradually finish more books. The objective is to make reading a natural part of your routine rather than another demanding task on your to-do list.

4. Practise gratitude before sleeping

Before going to bed, spend a few minutes thinking about three things you appreciated during the day. They do not have to be major achievements. It could be a meaningful conversation, a productive afternoon, a good meal, or simply having time to rest.

You can also write these moments in a small journal. This practice encourages you to pay attention to positive experiences instead of focusing only on what went wrong. Over time, it can help you develop a more appreciative outlook towards everyday life.

5. Drink a glass of water after waking up

After several hours of sleep without drinking water, having a glass of water in the morning can be a simple way to begin your day. Keep a glass or bottle near your bedside or in the kitchen so that it is easy to remember.

This small action can help you establish a regular hydration routine, particularly if you often forget to drink enough water during busy hours. It takes less than a minute but can become a useful part of your morning routine.

6. Spend five minutes decluttering your space

A cluttered desk, overflowing wardrobe or untidy workspace can make everyday tasks feel more overwhelming. Instead of waiting for an entire weekend to organise everything, spend five minutes putting things back in their proper places.

Clear your desk, arrange your books, remove unnecessary papers or organise items you frequently use. You do not need to clean your entire home at once. Small daily efforts can help prevent clutter from building up and make your surroundings easier to manage.

A quick read on a similar topic...

Declutter your life with ease: A simple 3-step method

7. Take a short walk without your phone

A short walk can give you a break from screens, notifications and continuous mental stimulation. Spend three to five minutes walking around your home, office or nearby outdoor space without checking your phone.

Use this time to observe your surroundings, breathe comfortably and give your mind a little break. Although a short walk cannot replace regular physical activity, it can be a useful way to introduce more movement into a sedentary routine.

Final thoughts

Improving your life does not always require dramatic changes or complicated routines. Sometimes, it begins with making your bed, reading two pages, drinking a glass of water or taking a few minutes to plan your day.

The beauty of micro-habits is that they make consistency feel achievable. You do not have to find an extra hour in your schedule or wait until your circumstances become perfect. You can start with a single action and gradually build upon it. Choose two or three habits from this list and practise them every day. Once they become part of your routine, introduce a few more.

Remember, a better year is not necessarily built through one extraordinary decision. It can begin with five minutes of intentional effort, repeated every day.

item.title: Gen Z’s guide to self-improvement: Build habits that pay off
item.description: Explore practical self-improvement habits for Gen Z that improve focus, confidence, productivity and personal growth while delivering long-term results.
item.content:encoded:
Self-improvement is everywhere, especially on social media. From morning routines and fitness challenges to productivity hacks and financial goals, Gen Z is constantly exposed to ways of becoming a better version of themselves. But with so much advice available, it can be difficult to know which habits are actually worth the effort.

The truth is that personal growth does not require a complete lifestyle makeover. It comes from small, consistent actions that create meaningful results over time. Instead of following every new trend, Gen Z can focus on habits that improve everyday life, strengthen skills and support long-term goals.

7 Practical self-improvement habits that offer a real return on effort

1. Set goals that have a clear purpose

Self-improvement becomes easier when you know what you are working towards. Rather than setting vague goals such as becoming successful or more productive, identify specific outcomes you want to achieve. It could be learning a professional skill, improving your fitness, saving money or reading more books.

Break larger goals into smaller steps and give yourself a realistic timeline. When you understand why a goal matters, it becomes easier to stay committed and measure your progress.

2. Learn skills that improve your future opportunities

In a competitive job market, learning beyond formal education can make a meaningful difference. Gen Z can invest time in practical skills such as communication, writing, digital marketing, financial literacy, data analysis or using AI tools responsibly.

You do not need to master everything at once. Choose one skill that supports your career or personal interests and practise it regularly. Free online courses, tutorials and hands-on projects can help you build knowledge without spending a fortune.

3. Build a routine that protects your focus

Constant notifications, social media and multitasking can make it difficult to concentrate. A simple daily routine can help you use your time more intentionally.

Start by identifying your most important tasks and completing them before getting distracted by less urgent activities. You can also set aside specific periods for studying, working, exercising and relaxing. The goal is not to follow a perfect schedule but to create a routine that makes your day easier to manage.

4. Develop better money habits early

Financial independence is an important part of personal growth. Developing healthy money habits early can help Gen Z make better decisions as their income and responsibilities increase.

Start by tracking your expenses, setting a monthly budget and saving a portion of your income whenever possible. Learn the basics of emergency funds, interest, debt and long-term investing before making financial decisions. Even small savings can build discipline and provide greater financial security over time.

5. Read and learn beyond social media

Social media can introduce you to new ideas, but meaningful learning requires more than scrolling through short videos and posts. Reading books, listening to educational podcasts and exploring reliable resources can help you develop a deeper understanding of different subjects.

You do not have to finish an entire book every week. Start with a few pages a day or spend 15 minutes learning something useful. Consistent learning can gradually improve your vocabulary, critical thinking and ability to make informed decisions.

6. Take care of your physical and mental well-being

Productivity should not come at the cost of your health. Regular movement, balanced meals, adequate sleep and time away from screens are essential parts of sustainable self-improvement.

Make realistic changes instead of following extreme fitness or wellness trends. Take a walk, maintain a consistent sleep schedule and make room for activities that help you relax. Taking care of yourself can support better concentration, energy and emotional well-being.

Also Read
Doom-scrolling detox: 7 Simple rules to reclaim your attention

7. Track progress instead of chasing perfection

One reason people give up on self-improvement is that they expect immediate results. However, meaningful changes often take time. Missing a workout, delaying a task or breaking a routine does not mean you have failed.

Keep track of your progress through a journal, habit tracker or weekly review. Notice what is working, identify what needs improvement and adjust your approach when necessary. Focus on becoming more consistent rather than trying to achieve perfection every day.

Final thoughts

For Gen Z, self-improvement should be less about following every productivity trend and more about making choices that create lasting value. The best habits are not necessarily the most impressive ones; they are the ones that make everyday life better.

Whether it is learning a new skill, managing money, protecting your focus or prioritising health, every small effort can contribute to long-term growth. Instead of asking how quickly you can transform your life, ask which habits will continue to benefit you months or even years from now.

That is the real return on effort: building a life where today's small actions create tomorrow's opportunities.

item.title: EPFO approves systematic withdrawal plan for retiring members
item.description: Retiring members can now opt for receiving their retirement savings in periodic installments instead of a lump sum amount.
item.content:encoded:
The retirement fund body Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) on Thursday approved a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for its retiring members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire corpus at once.

Under the SWP, retiring members of the EPFO will receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic installments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once, a Labour Ministry release said.

The decision was taken at the 240th meeting of the Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF), chaired by Union Minister for Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, Mansukh Mandaviya.

The Board approved a proposal to introduce a Systematic Withdrawal Plan, enabling retiring EPF members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic installments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once.

This reform will enable retiring members to withdraw their accumulated provident fund savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.

This facility would provide members with a structured source of periodic income while allowing the remaining corpus to continue generating returns, thereby helping augment their retirement income and supplement their pension benefits.

The facility would be entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals.

The option may also be extended to eligible family members/beneficiaries, ensuring greater flexibility and financial security for the family. This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability, and extend social security coverage to gig and platform workers.

SWP will enable members to convert their retirement savings into a stable and predictable stream of systematic withdrawals post-retirement, while preserving ownership of the underlying corpus.

Approximately 6.32 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years with provident fund accumulations exceeding Rs 5 lakh are expected to be the primary beneficiaries of the proposed SWP framework during the initial phase.

item.title: 'Where are the jobs?' Modi tells industry to respond to tax relief with hiring, salary hikes
item.description: Prime Minister Narendra Modi lamented that despite reforms in areas of corporate tax, income tax and GST, it has not resulted in job creation by the industry.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday questioned industry leaders over the lack of commensurate job creation and salary increases despite the government's tax concessions, challenging businesses to translate higher consumer purchasing power into greater employment and economic activity.

Addressing the FICCI annual general meeting here, Modi said the government had taken several steps to improve the business environment, including reducing the basic corporate tax rate from 30% in 2014 to 22%, simplifying tax return and refund processes and lowering GST rates on several products.

"I know you won't applaud. I know that very well, because your appetite is so enormous that no matter how much you are given, it is never enough," he told industry leaders. "I have given income tax relief up to Rs 12 lakh. But have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you increased the number of employees? No! It is always: 'Modi ji, you do it; we will see what happens.' This is how things will continue."

He also cited the income-tax exemption for annual incomes of up to Rs 12 lakh, saying the relief had boosted people's purchasing power and should translate into greater demand and business expansion.

"How much ever you give, their appetite is never satisfied," Modi said in a pointed remark to industry leaders, adding that businesses needed to do more for their employees rather than expect the government to shoulder the responsibility for growth.

He said a country could progress only by respecting its farmers, small entrepreneurs, industries, wealth creators and taxpayers, and not by criticising them.

"No country can progress unless it respects its farmers, small entrepreneurs, industries, wealth creators and taxpayers. A country cannot move forward by abusing them morning and evening," he said.

Modi recalled a gathering of the income tax department in Gujarat way back in 2001-02. He had become Chief Minister of Gujarat then.

"I did not understand much at the time; I had little knowledge and no experience either. But I delivered a speech there. This must have been around 2001-02, perhaps 25 years ago. All the senior officials of the Income Tax Department were present. I asked them: 'When will you stop treating everyone as a thief? What kind of approach is this? You, too, work for the country. Are we the only ones who have taken it upon ourselves to serve the nation? You also do your bit, and every citizen does their bit. Everyone deserves respect.'"

The Prime Minister also cautioned businesses against treating India's large domestic market as an assured source of sales, saying companies must improve product quality and become globally competitive.

"Do not consider the 140 crore Indians an assured market," he said, urging industry to shed the mindset that whatever it produces will automatically find buyers in the domestic market.

He criticised the practice of marketing products as "export quality" to Indian consumers, asking whether people in the country did not deserve the same quality as overseas customers.

"My countrymen deserve quality," he said.

Modi urged Indian businesses to take advantage of the trade agreements signed by India with several countries, saying these had opened doors to major global markets.

He described the agreements as a historic opportunity for Indian industry and asked businesses whether they had prepared plans to tap the new markets.

item.title: Cyient Semiconductors bags $10M from GlobalFoundries
item.description: Cyient Semiconductors will use the capital to scale custom-chip development, manufacturing access, and global growth.
item.content:encoded:
Cyient Semiconductors has secured $10 million equity investment from GlobalFoundries, a global semiconductor manufacturer serving the data centre, automotive, and communications markets.

Hyderabad-headquartered Cyient said the investment carries the same pre-money valuation of $490 million as its recent financing led by Edelweiss, taking its combined post-money valuation to $510 million.

However, the announcement does not explain the calculation behind the combined valuation. The Edelweiss round in May involved approximately $10 million in equity from funds managed by EAAA India Alternatives and affiliated co-investors, alongside structured debt.

The freshly raised capital will be used to expand Cyient's turnkey custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) capabilities, accelerate custom silicon development, and improve long-term access to wafers, the silicon discs on which chips are manufactured.

Suman Narayan, Chief Executive Officer of Cyient Semiconductors, said the investment would help the company accelerate innovation, strengthen engineering capabilities, and scale global customer engagements. He described the funding as “a strong validation” of the opportunity for semiconductor innovation from India.

Cyient develops ASICs, chips designed for particular products or functions, as well as power-management products. Its capabilities span chip architecture, design, manufacturing coordination, packaging, testing and qualification. Its customers operate across the automotive, industrial, artificial intelligence, communications and data centre markets.

The company follows a fabless model, meaning it designs chips but relies on specialist manufacturers, known as foundries, to produce them. GlobalFoundries' (GF) involvement is significant in this respect. The companies had already established a channel partnership in August 2025 to provide customers with access to GF’s semiconductor manufacturing services and technologies.

Cyient has also been expanding its product portfolio. In April, it completed an $85 million majority investment in Kinetic Technologies, adding more than 250 power-management and related products, alongside established customer relationships and semiconductor intellectual property.

The latest investment comes amid growing interest in India’s chip-design sector. In February, Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors raised $15 million in a Series A round led by Peak XV Partners, while Vervesemi Microelectronics secured $10 million from investors including Ashish Kacholia and Unicorn India Ventures. Both companies are developing chips for applications spanning AI infrastructure, power management, and industrial systems.

However, semiconductor businesses typically require substantial research and development spending and longer periods to bring products to commercial scale, making sustained funding important.

Government support is also expanding. In July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of Rs 1.275 lakh crore, covering chip design, manufacturing equipment and materials, fabrication plants, advanced packaging, research, and talent development.

In November, the government opened applications for support covering equipment and materials, new fabrication facilities, and semiconductor assembly and testing. Of the 12 projects approved under the first phase of the India Semiconductor Mission, five had commenced commercial production by October.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Style Union raises Rs 485 Cr to expand beyond southern India
item.description: Style Union’s parent has raised Rs 485 crore from Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners to expand nationally, targeting 450 stores by March 2030.
item.content:encoded:
Nexon Omniverse Limited, the parent company of value-fashion retailer Style Union, has raised Rs 485 crore in a Series E round led by Venturi Partners, a consumer-focused investment firm, and co-led by Elev8 Venture Partners, a growth-stage investor.

The funding comprises primary and secondary capital, but the company has not disclosed the split.

The money will support expansion beyond Style Union’s southern base into western and northern India, the company said. The company also plans to grow from 200 stores to 220 by March 2027 and 450 by March 2030. 

Whole-time director Rajesh Seth called the investment an endorsement of its effort to make “quality fashion at fair prices” a profitable business. He said the next phase would take the brand into new cities and households.

Launched in 2022, Style Union sells affordable family fashion across eight states and Delhi-NCR. The company said it expanded from 41 stores and Rs 123 crore in net revenue in FY23 to 158 stores and more than Rs 1,150 crore in revenue in FY26. 

Venturi founder Nicholas Cator said the company treats value as “a promise, not a price point”. Elev8’s Navin Honagudi cited its focus on “unit economics” and disciplined inventory management.

The fundraise comes as value fashion gains ground. Crisil Ratings expects organised apparel retailers to grow revenue by 12-13% in FY27. It found value fashion’s share of organised apparel revenue rose from 39% to 46% in three years, with the segment growing more than twice as fast as others. 

However, higher cotton and operating costs, alongside intense competition, could squeeze margins. CareEdge estimates India’s apparel retail market will reach Rs 16 lakh crore by FY30. Organised retail accounts for about 41% of the market and is projected to grow by 10-13%.

Other fashion businesses have attracted capital too. The Pant Project raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B round led by Mirae Asset in October 2026 to expand stores and product categories. Design-led brand Theater secured Rs 75 crore in September for offline expansion.

Meanwhile, policy changes may support affordable apparel. Since September 2025, readymade garments priced up to Rs 2,500 per piece have attracted 5% GST, extending the earlier threshold of Rs 1,000. 

The textile production-linked incentive scheme was also revised to halve the minimum investment requirement, lower the incremental turnover criterion from 25% to 10%, and add 17 man-made-fibre apparel and fabric products. The scheme targets manufacturers rather than retailers directly.

item.title: From pattern matching to governing intent: How Semantic DLP is securing enterprise Gen AI
item.description: Legacy DLP was built to catch patterns. It was not built to understand what employees paste into AI. Wald.ai, part of NetApp Excellerator’s Cohort 15, is teaching security to read intent.
item.content:encoded:
A quiet tug-of-war is playing out in nearly every enterprise today. On one hand, engineers, financial analysts, legal teams, and operations staff are turning to generative and agentic AI to debug code, summarize contracts, and automate tasks and decision-making. On the other side, security and compliance leaders are racing to prevent proprietary source code, financial projections, and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized models.

For most Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs), the question is no longer whether employees are using AI; it is what they are pasting into it. Yet the security tools most organizations rely on to police this boundary were built for a completely different era.

Why legacy DLP fails in the GenAI era

Traditional Data Loss Prevention (DLP) systems were designed for structured data moving across predictable channels such as emails, file transfers, and cloud storage. They rely heavily on regular expressions (regex), keyword lists, and static rules. If a document contains a 16-digit credit card number or a government ID, legacy DLP flags it.

Generative AI breaks this model entirely. AI interactions happen in unstructured natural language, where data sensitivity is defined by context and intent rather than fixed formatting. Consider two scenarios:

  • A software engineer pastes a snippet of proprietary authentication logic into an LLM and asks it to optimize the code.
  • A strategy analyst uploads a paragraph describing an upcoming, unannounced product roadmap or M&A target to draft an executive summary.

Neither prompt contains a credit card number, a Social Security number, or a flagged keyword. To a regex-based DLP system, both interactions look completely benign. Conversely, when security teams tighten keyword rules to catch more nuances, false positives skyrocket, triggering alert fatigue for security teams and frustrating employees who are simply trying to do their jobs.

Faced with this visibility gap, many organizations initially defaulted to blunt-force bans on public AI tools. However, blocking AI only drives usage underground onto personal devices and unsanctioned accounts, multiplying “Shadow AI” risk while starving the enterprise of productivity gains.

The shift to semantic, context-aware security

As generative AI evolves from simple chat interfaces to complex, autonomous workflows including Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls and agent-to-agent communications, the enterprise attack surface is expanding across every endpoint and application. Securing this environment requires moving from pattern matching to semantic understanding.

At Wald.ai, we built our platform around a simple premise: to secure AI, your security layer must understand language as well as the AI itself.

Instead of scanning for static patterns, Semantic DLP evaluates the meaning, context, and intent behind every prompt and file upload. By deploying a specialized Small Language Model (SLM) directly on the employee’s endpoint, Wald.ai inspects and classifies AI interactions locally in milliseconds before sensitive data ever traverses the network or reaches an external AI server or provider.

This on-device, context-aware approach solves three critical enterprise challenges simultaneously:

1. Catching what Regex misses: Semantic models distinguish between an engineer pasting harmless open-source boilerplate and one exposing proprietary algorithms, or between general market research and confidential corporate strategy.

2. Eliminating alert fatigue: By disambiguating context in real time, organizations drastically reduce false positives, allowing security teams to focus on genuine exposure risks.

3. Enabling safe productivity at the endpoint: Rather than a binary “allow or block” posture, enterprises can enforce granular, real-time guardrails, automatically redacting, masking, or sanitizing sensitive entities within a prompt while preserving the context needed for the LLM to return a useful answer.

Real-world impact across regulated sectors

We are already seeing this playbook transform how regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, and legal practices adopt AI. For instance, financial institutions and credit unions using Wald.ai have transitioned from restrictive AI policies to sanctioned, company-wide adoption.

Scaling enterprise AI governance with NetApp Excellerator

As enterprises mature in their AI journey, the boundary between data infrastructure and AI security is disappearing. Participating in Cohort 15 of the NetApp Excellerator program has been a pivotal milestone for Wald.ai as it scales contextual intelligence architecture for large enterprise environments.

Working alongside NetApp’s technology leaders and deep-tech ecosystem provided insights into how global enterprises architect, govern, and manage massive data estates across hybrid and cloud environments. Combining robust data infrastructure practices with real-time, endpoint semantic guardrails ensures that data remains protected from the storage layer all the way to the AI prompt.

The road ahead

The next wave of enterprise competitiveness will not be won by the companies that restrict AI, nor by those that deploy it recklessly. It will be won by organizations that build trust into their AI stack, replacing outdated, reactive compliance checks with intelligent guardrails that operate at the speed of conversation. When security understands context, enterprises no longer have to choose between innovation and data privacy.

item.title: When agents go out of bounds: How Lasso is helping enterprises secure the AI agents they build and use
item.description: Enterprises are deploying AI agents faster than they can track them, and not every agent stays within the boundaries it was given. Lasso, part of NetApp Excellerator, is changing that.
item.content:encoded:
An AI agent handling a refund request starts a funds transfer that no one asked for and no one approved. Would the company notice before the money moved?

This is the problem Lasso is addressing. Part of the NetApp Excellerator program, it protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, by learning what each agent is meant to do and checking every action it takes against that purpose.

Enterprises are putting AI agents to work faster than they can keep track of them. These agents plan their own steps, call tools and MCP servers on their own, and act without a person approving each move. That autonomy is the reason companies deploy them, and it is also how an agent ends up outside the boundaries it was given.

Two challenges make this hard to control.

The challenges of securing AI agents

Agents are everywhere, and each one has its own purpose. AI agents now run in every part of the enterprise. Developers use coding assistants on their endpoints and connect them to MCP servers and skills. Engineering teams build custom agents that run in code and in the cloud, and business teams create their own agent using low-code no-code builder platforms.

Each of these agents are set up for a different purpose, and each one works toward it autonomously. With this many agents running in this many places, it becomes difficult to track what any single agent is meant to do, and without that there is no reliable way to tell when one has gone off task or gone rogue.

Context windows are large, and attacks hide inside them

Each agent gathers the context it needs for a task by calling models, MCP servers, tools, and data sources, and everything it gathers goes into its context window. For a single task, that context can reach hundreds of thousands of tokens. A prompt injection can be one sentence hidden in an email, a web page, or a tool response, and inside a context that large it becomes the needle in the haystack. Most detection models were built for short prompts. On inputs of this size, they slow down or miss the attack, and an agent that reads the injected instruction may act on it as if it came from the user.

How Lasso does it

Lasso’s AI security platform protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, whether that is on an endpoint, in code or in the cloud.

It works from each agent’s intent. Its Intent Security Engine learns what each agent is meant to do from its configuration and its history, and it checks every action the agent takes against that purpose.

An action that does not fit, such as a support agent starting a funds transfer in the middle of a refund conversation, is flagged, masked or blocked inline in under 50 milliseconds, with 98.6% detection accuracy. Because the check is made against the agent’s purpose, it catches an agent that has gone off task even when nothing in the request looks like a known attack.

Lasso’s detection is built for the size of agentic inputs. It holds the same accuracy and latency as the context grows toward a million tokens, so an injection hidden deep in a long input is found before the agent acts on it.

The Lasso platform

The platform covers the full path from finding an agent to protecting it in production.

  • Discovery finds every AI agent, model and component in use across SaaS tools, code, cloud and agent builder platforms.
  • AI-BOM gives each agent a bill of materials listing the models, MCP servers, tools and components it depends on, so a vulnerable component can be traced to every agent that uses it.
  • AI-SPM maps each agent’s connections in a visual graph that shows its blast radius, checks configurations against NIST, OWASP and MITRE, and limits use to approved models and components.
  • Automated AI Red Teaming tests agents the way an attacker would. Reconnaissance of each agent shapes static, dynamic and high-agency attacks drawn from more than 300,000 payloads, and the tests run in CI/CD on every deployment.
  • Runtime Protection and AI Detection and Response enforce policy per agent at the SDK, API or AI Gateway layer and detect prompt injection and other OWASP and MITRE risks. Each alert explains what happened, which agent was targeted and what to do next.
  • Rogue Agent Protection uses the Intent Security Engine to detect goal misalignment, intent drift and behavioral anomalies, and it stops an agent’s action when it moves outside its purpose.

Customer success stories

A European insurance group runs Lasso on the production agents that process its internal claims, where prompt injection attempts arrive embedded inside the claims documents themselves. Lasso blocks them before the agents act. The company has since moved the application to production and is adding hundreds of new agents.

A global hospitality company uses Lasso to secure the agents it built for employee-facing logistics workflows. Intent-based guardrails enforce each agent’s behavior in real time, and the company’s internal MCP-based use cases were secured without code changes.

A global automotive manufacturer runs Lasso’s runtime protection across its customer-facing systems to stop jailbreak attempts and sensitive data exposure. A red teaming engagement on a separate chatbot found more than 15 vulnerabilities that had gone undetected, and all of them were fixed before they could be exploited.

item.title: InPrime Finserv raises Rs 101 Cr in Series B round led by FMO
item.description: InPrime will use the funding to expand its reach and improve its technology stack, especially in AI use cases.
item.content:encoded:
InPrime Finserv, a tech-led NBFC, has raised Rs 101 crore in a Series B funding round led by FMO, the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank. This round also saw participation from existing investors Z47 and Pravega Ventures.

InPrime will utilise the capital to expand the reach of existing products and diversify into micro-mortgage products, in line with its segment-focused lending approach. The NBFC will also deepen its investments in AI-driven use cases, across agentic AI and co-pilots.

“From the beginning, we have believed that prime customers are not limited to the formal economy. We have been building around the evolving needs of India’s informal prime customers by combining engineering, local presence and relevant financial products.,” said Rajat Singh, Co-founder and CEO, InPrime Finserv.

InPrime operates 46 area offices across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh. It has served 27,000+ households and has disbursed Rs 516.92 crore to date. As of September 30, 2026, its assets under management stood at Rs 332.8 crore, with gross non-performing assets of 0.80%.

Founded in 2021 by Sneh Thakur, Manish Raj and Rajat Singh, InPrime is focused on customers who do not fall under the category of formal employment. This NBFC believes that despite the credit worthiness of this segment, they are unable to raise loans due to the traditional practices of lenders.

According to InPrime, its technology stack allows it to effectively do the task of credit underwriting, which requires interpreting unstructured data, understanding customers beyond conventional financial metrics, and delivering services at scale in vernacular languages.

“Expanding access to finance for underserved entrepreneurs and households is closely aligned with FMO’s aim of making finance more inclusive and accessible. InPrime’s combination of technology, data-driven underwriting, and local presence provides an opportunity to reach customers who are often overlooked by traditional lenders,” said Peter Byrde, Director Private Equity at FMO.
